cards.why: The mechanism of religious conquest by absorption — Buddhist missionaries did not refute Shinto's gods, they reclassified them as local forms of Buddhas, producing Ryobu Shinto.
cards.uw: When a new system wants to win without a fight, watch for reclassification — the old gods survive by becoming avatars of the new ones.
cards.book: Shinto: The Ancient Religion of Japan — William George Aston

cards.title: Shinto is doomed to extinction
cards.steal: Without a code of morals, or an efficient ecclesiastical organisation, with little aid from the arts of painting, sculpture, and architecture, and with a sacred literature scanty and feeble compared with those of its foreign rivals, Shinto is doomed to extinction.
cards.why: Aston's 1921 closing verdict — delivered with total confidence, and worth keeping as a card precisely because history gets to grade it: the religion he buried is still alive.
cards.uw: When an expert declares a living tradition dead, keep the receipt — Aston wrote the obituary in 1921 and the patient survived him.
cards.book: Shinto: The Ancient Religion of Japan — William George Aston

cards.title: From successful defense to problematic offense: the devolution of unconventional warfare
cards.book: From successful defense to problematic offense: the devolution of unconventional warfare — Timothy S. Ball
cards.steal: Unconventional warfare began in World War II as a defensive tactic for assisting an occupied ally, but Special Forces later redefined it to include offensive regime change; offensive UW, practiced extensively by the CIA during the Cold War, produced poor results, and it remains problematic — unreliable proxy forces, unpredictable outcomes, negative international perception. Defensive UW, under certain conditions, remains justified and practical.
cards.why: It names the mechanism behind every proxy-war debate — backing someone else's fighters looks cheap until the proxies, the blowback, and the perception bill arrive. The CIA's own 2014 study (cited in the thesis) found arming rebels seldom works.
cards.uw: Offense by proxy inherits everyone else's agency — if you can't vet the proxy, you can't own the outcome.

cards.title: Empirical analysis of using erasure coding in outsourcing data storage with provable security
cards.book: Empirical analysis of using erasure coding in outsourcing data storage with provable security — Abdallah Bakir
cards.steal: Proof of retrievability (POR) and proof of data possession (PDP) are cryptographic auditing tools that give probabilistic guarantees a server or cloud is actually storing your data — without downloading the whole file — and can recover the original data under certain limits; maximum distance separable (MDS) codes, specifically Reed-Solomon and Cauchy Reed-Solomon, are the recoverability engine, and the thesis surveys them and implements both into a prototype POR library built on the liberasurecode library.
cards.why: Every "is my cloud copy intact?" guarantee rests on this primitive — verifying petabytes without re-downloading them is what makes outsourced storage auditable instead of faith-based.
cards.uw: You don't need to hold the whole thing to prove it's intact — probabilistic proof beats full inspection; audit at the cheapest level that still binds.

cards.title: A Validation of the Proposed Royal Australian Navy Standard Work Week and Naval Management Diary Using a Simulated Crew of an Armidale Class Patrol Boat
cards.book: A Validation of the Proposed Royal Australian Navy Standard Work Week and Naval Management Diary Using a Simulated Crew of an Armidale Class Patrol Boat — Jessica Groot (Lieutenant
cards.steal: Simulating a 21-member Armidale-class patrol boat crew in the Navy Management Diary over three weeks, the proposed RAN Navy Standard Work Week model breaks down in practice — the maintenance category most often exceeded its allocated hours, which the thesis says may warrant platform- and occupation-specific customization; and the NMD's fatigue tool versus the SAFTE model (FAST software) produced statistically significant differences in predicted risk, so the methodology should be replicated on a larger sample with real operational performance observations before comparing the two.
cards.why: A work-week policy that looks fine on a spreadsheet and fails at the maintenance line is how a navy discovers fatigue in the field instead of on paper — the thesis is an argument that crew-endurance models must be validated against operations, not against each other.
cards.uw: When two validated-looking models disagree significantly, the answer isn't to pick one — it's to test both against reality.

cards.title: The West kept reforming instead of dying
cards.steal: Western Civilization, on the contrary, did not pass from the Age of Crisis to the Age of Universal Empire, but instead was able to reform itself and entered upon a new period of expansion. Moreover, Western Civilization did this not once, but several times. It was this ability to reform or reorganize itself again and again which made Western Civilization the dominant factor in the world at the beginning of the twentieth century.
cards.why: Quigley's whole theory pivots here: every other civilization went expansion, crisis, universal empire, decay — the West broke the cycle by reorganizing itself, repeatedly, instead of consolidating into one empire.
cards.uw: When someone declares a civilization finished because its growth slowed — ask whether it is dying or reorganizing.
cards.book: Tragedy and Hope — Carroll Quigley

cards.title: The four marks of an Age of Conflict
cards.steal: (a) it is a period of declining rate of expansion; (b) it is a period of growing tensions and class conflicts; (c) it is a period of increasingly frequent and increasingly violent imperialist wars; and (d) it is a period of growing irrationality, pessimism, superstitions, and otherworldliness.
cards.why: A diagnostic checklist for civilizational stall: the economics slow first, then the politics turn violent, then the culture turns superstitious — in that order, core before periphery.
cards.uw: When growth stalls and the culture war gets weirder at the same time — check the sequence, not just the symptoms.
cards.book: Tragedy and Hope — Carroll Quigley

cards.title: Expansion petrifies into vested interests
cards.steal: In time, this system of commercial capitalism became petrified into a structure of vested interests in which profits were sought by imposing restrictions on the production or interchange of goods rather than by encouraging these activities.
cards.why: The engine of every Quigley cycle: the organization that created the expansion hardens into the thing blocking the next one — profit shifts from making more to guarding what exists.
cards.uw: When an industry's profits come from blocking entrants rather than serving customers — you are looking at petrification, not competition.
cards.book: Tragedy and Hope — Carroll Quigley

cards.title: Four capitalists, four profit sources
cards.steal: The commercial capitalist sought profits from the exchange of goods; the industrial capitalist sought profits from the manufacture of goods; the financial capitalist sought profits from the manipulation of claims on money; and the monopoly capitalist sought profits from manipulation of the market to make the market price and the amount sold such that his profits would be maximized.
cards.why: Quigley's cleanest taxonomy: each stage of capitalism is defined by where profit is extracted — and each stage's profit source becomes the next stage's target for capture.
cards.uw: When classifying a business or an era — ask where the profit actually comes from, not what the brochure says.
cards.book: Tragedy and Hope — Carroll Quigley

cards.title: The financial capitalists at their worst
cards.steal: The outbreak of war in 1914 showed these financial capitalists at their worst, narrow in outlook, ignorant, and selfish, while proclaiming, as usual, their total devotion to the social good.
cards.why: Quigley, the insider-sympathizer, delivers his harshest verdict on the bankers at the exact moment their system met reality — expertise as performance, self-interest as public service.
cards.uw: When the experts' models say a crisis is impossible and it happens anyway — remember who the models served.
cards.book: Tragedy and Hope — Carroll Quigley

cards.title: Wars are not fought with gold
cards.steal: Wars, as events have proved since, are not fought with gold or even with money, but by the proper organization of real resources.
cards.why: The bankers' 1914 prediction — that the war must end in months for lack of gold — exposed the core fallacy: money is the scoreboard, organization is the game.
cards.uw: When finance people explain why something cannot be done — check whether they are describing money or reality.
cards.book: Tragedy and Hope — Carroll Quigley

cards.title: Four ways to pay for a war
cards.steal: a. Taxation gives no inflation and no debt. b. Fiat money gives inflation and no debt. c. Bank credit gives inflation and debt. d. Sales of bonds give no inflation but give debt.
cards.why: Sixteen words that decode a century of war finance: every government's funding mix is a choice about who pays — present taxpayers, savers, or the unborn.
cards.uw: When a government announces how it will fund a crisis — run it through the four cells and see who is really paying.
cards.book: Tragedy and Hope — Carroll Quigley

cards.title: A world system of financial control in private hands
cards.steal: the powers of financial capitalism had another far-reaching aim, nothing less than to create a world system of financial control in private hands able to dominate the political system of each country and the economy of the world as a whole. This system was to be controlled in a feudalist fashion by the central banks of the world acting in concert, by secret agreements arrived at in frequent private meetings and conferences.
cards.why: Quigley's most-quoted claim, stated as the bankers' own program: not conspiracy theory but institutional design — private, feudal, coordinated through central banks, apexed at the BIS in Basle.
cards.uw: When central bankers meet in Basle and markets move on the minutes — this is the architecture Quigley described.
cards.book: Tragedy and Hope — Carroll Quigley

cards.title: How central banks dominate governments
cards.steal: Each central bank, in the hands of men like Montagu Norman of the Bank of England, Benjamin Strong of the New York Federal Reserve Bank, Charles Rist of the Bank of France, and Hjalmar Schacht of the Reichsbank, sought to dominate its government by its ability to control Treasury loans, to manipulate foreign exchanges, to influence the level of economic activity in the country, and to influence cooperative politicians by subsequent economic rewards in the business world.
cards.why: The mechanism, named with names: dominance through Treasury loans, exchange manipulation, the business cycle itself — and the revolving door as the enforcement arm.
cards.uw: When a central banker becomes a political oracle — ask which of the four levers is doing the talking.
cards.book: Tragedy and Hope — Carroll Quigley

cards.title: The BIS: a private bank owned by central banks
cards.steal: The B.I.S. as a private institution was owned by the seven chief central banks and was operated by the heads of these, who together formed its governing board. They made agreements on all the major financial problems of the world, as well as on many of the economic and political problems, especially in reference to loans, payments, and the economic future of the chief areas of the globe.
cards.why: The apex of Quigley's system in one paragraph: a private bank, owned by central banks that were themselves private corporations, settling the world's money by bookkeeping instead of shipping gold.
cards.uw: When someone says central banks are public institutions — the BIS charter says otherwise.
cards.book: Tragedy and Hope — Carroll Quigley

cards.title: Rhodes's aim: federate the English-speaking peoples
cards.steal: These purposes centered on his desire to federate the English-speaking peoples and to bring all the habitable portions of the world under their control. For this purpose Rhodes left part of his great fortune to found the Rhodes Scholarships at Oxford in order to spread the English ruling class tradition throughout the English-speaking world as Ruskin had wanted.
cards.why: The motive behind the network, in Quigley's telling: the Rhodes Scholarships were not philanthropy but a personnel system — training an imperial ruling class under the cover of education.
cards.uw: When an elite fellowship claims to be about merit — ask what ruling tradition it was built to spread.
cards.book: Tragedy and Hope — Carroll Quigley

cards.title: The secret society of February 5, 1891
cards.steal: This association was formally established on February 5, 1891, when Rhodes and Stead organized a secret society of which Rhodes had been dreaming for sixteen years. In this secret society Rhodes was to be leader; Stead, Brett (Lord Esher), and Milner were to form an executive committee; Arthur (Lord) Balfour, (Sir) Harry Johnston, Lord Rothschild, Albert (Lord) Grey, and others were listed as potential members of a "Circle of Initiates"; while there was to be an outer circle known as the "Association of Helpers" (later organized by Milner as the Round Table organization).
cards.why: Quigley's documentary core for the network claim: a dated founding, a named executive committee, a Circle of Initiates, and an outer circle that became the Round Table — the organizational chart of the Anglo-American establishment.
cards.uw: When tracing how an idea becomes policy across decades — look for the personnel network, not just the institutions.
cards.book: Tragedy and Hope — Carroll Quigley

cards.title: Five outlooks, from Enlightenment to Inclusive Diversity
cards.steal: Over the past two centuries, there have been five such stages: the Enlightenment in 1730-1790, the Romantic Movement in 1790-1850, the Age of Scientific Materialism in 1850-1895, the Period of Irrational Activism of 1895-1945, and our new Age of Inclusive Diversity since 1945.
cards.why: Quigley's cultural periodization: the twentieth century's new outlook is not a doctrine but a condition — diversity as the operating system, replacing the materialist certainties that ended in 1945.
cards.uw: When a debate feels like two centuries talking past each other — check which outlook each side inhabits.
cards.book: Tragedy and Hope — Carroll Quigley

cards.title: The twentieth century began in 1950
cards.steal: The time covered by this book seems to this historian to fall into three periods: the nineteenth century from about 1814 to about 1895; the twentieth century, which did not begin until after World War II, perhaps as late as 1950; and a long period of transition from 1895 to 1950.
cards.why: Quigley's dating refuses the calendar: the 'twentieth century' is not 1900-1999 but the postwar order — and 1895-1950 was a 55-year transition, one of the most awful periods in all human history.
cards.uw: When periodizing any era — date it by the system change, not the round number.
cards.book: Tragedy and Hope — Carroll Quigley

cards.title: War and depression are man-made, and needless
cards.steal: The hope of the twentieth century rests on its recognition that war and depression are man-made, and needless.
cards.why: The entire 1,300-page tragedy compressed into the hope: if the catastrophes were made by human choices, they can be unmade by human choices — the book's title in one sentence.
cards.uw: When catastrophe is framed as inevitable — ask who made it, and who benefits from the framing.
cards.book: Tragedy and Hope — Carroll Quigley

cards.title: The nineteenth century's epitaph
cards.steal: the nineteenth century was, however hopeful in its general processes, a period of materialism, selfishness, false values, hypocrisy, and secret vices.
cards.why: Quigley refuses nostalgia for the pre-1914 world: the horrors of 1914-1945 did not come from nowhere — they were the nineteenth century's underlying evils emerging 'in all their nakedness.'
cards.uw: When someone romanticizes a golden age — ask what evils were working underneath it.
cards.book: Tragedy and Hope — Carroll Quigley

cards.title: The international Anglophile network
cards.steal: There does exist, and has existed for a generation, an international Anglophile network which operates, to some extent, in the way the ... Right believes the Communists act. In fact, this network, which we may identify as the Round Table Groups, has no aversion to cooperating with the Communists, or any other groups, and frequently does so. I know of the operations of this network because I have studied it for twenty years and was permitted for two years, in the early 1960's, to examine its papers and secret records.
cards.why: The book's most famous admission, in Quigley's own voice: a named network — the Round Table Groups — operating internationally for a generation, studied by him for twenty years with two years of access to its papers and secret records.
cards.uw: When the establishment is dismissed as a figure of speech — Quigley studied this one for twenty years and read its secret records.
cards.book: Tragedy and Hope — Carroll Quigley
The Prince — Niccolò Machiavelli
cards.title: The naturalness of acquiring
cards.steal: The wish to acquire is in truth very natural and common, and men always do so when they can, and for this they will be praised not blamed; but when they cannot do so, yet wish to do so by any means, then there is folly and blame.
cards.why: Sets the book’s moral frame: expansion itself is natural and praiseworthy; only incompetent expansion is folly.
cards.uw: When someone moralizes ambition itself instead of how it is pursued.

cards.book: The Prince — Niccolò Machiavelli
cards.title: The innovator’s enemies
cards.steal: And it ought to be remembered that there is nothing more difficult to take in hand, more perilous to conduct, or more uncertain in its success, than to take the lead in the introduction of a new order of things, because the innovator has for enemies all those who have done well under the old conditions, and lukewarm defenders in those who may do well under the new.
cards.why: The original statement of why reform is hard: the old order’s beneficiaries fight, the new order’s beneficiaries don’t believe yet.
cards.uw: When a reform or reorg stalls and you need the mechanism, not the morale speech.
cards.source_locator: Chapter VI — Concerning New Principalities Which Are Acquired By One’s Own Arms And Ability

cards.book: The Prince — Niccolò Machiavelli
cards.title: Severities, properly used
cards.steal: Those may be called properly used, if of evil it is possible to speak well, that are applied at one blow and are necessary to one’s security, and that are not persisted in afterwards unless they can be turned to the advantage of the subjects.
cards.why: The economy of cruelty: all necessary harm at one stroke, then benefits; the drip-feed of harm is what loses states.
cards.uw: When debating whether to rip the bandage off.
cards.source_locator: Chapter VIII — Concerning Those Who Have Obtained A Principality By Wickedness

cards.book: The Prince — Niccolò Machiavelli
cards.title: The real truth of the matter
cards.steal: But, it being my intention to write a thing which shall be useful to him who apprehends it, it appears to me more appropriate to follow up the real truth of the matter than the imagination of it; for many have pictured republics and principalities which in fact have never been known or seen, because how one lives is so far distant from how one ought to live, that he who neglects what is done for what ought to be done, sooner effects his ruin than his preservation
cards.why: The book’s method in one line: study what is done, not what ought to be done, because the distance between them ruins the virtuous.
cards.uw: When a plan is built on how people should behave.
cards.source_locator: Chapter XV — Concerning Things For Which Men, And Especially Princes, Are Praised Or Blamed

cards.book: The Prince — Niccolò Machiavelli
cards.title: Feared, not loved
cards.steal: It may be answered that one should wish to be both, but, because it is difficult to unite them in one person, it is much safer to be feared than loved, when, of the two, either must be dispensed with. Because this is to be asserted in general of men, that they are ungrateful, fickle, false, cowardly, covetous, and as long as you succeed they are yours entirely; they will offer you their blood, property, life, and children, as is said above, when the need is far distant; but when it approaches they turn against you.
cards.why: Love is voluntary and fickle; fear is a bond you control. The cold logic of relying on other men’s promises.
cards.uw: When trust is being treated as a strategy.
cards.source_locator: Chapter XVII — Concerning Cruelty And Clemency, And Whether It Is Better To Be Loved Than Feared

cards.book: The Prince — Niccolò Machiavelli
cards.title: The fox and the lion
cards.steal: so it is necessary for a prince to know how to make use of both natures, and that one without the other is not durable. A prince, therefore, being compelled knowingly to adopt the beast, ought to choose the fox and the lion; because the lion cannot defend himself against snares and the fox cannot defend himself against wolves. Therefore, it is necessary to be a fox to discover the snares and a lion to terrify the wolves.
cards.why: Force without cunning walks into snares; cunning without force cannot hold what it takes. One without the other is not durable.
cards.uw: When someone is all-lawyer or all-muscle.
cards.source_locator: Chapter XVIII — Concerning The Way In Which Princes Should Keep Faith

cards.book: The Prince — Niccolò Machiavelli
cards.title: Judge by the result
cards.steal: Every one sees what you appear to be, few really know what you are, and those few dare not oppose themselves to the opinion of the many, who have the majesty of the state to defend them; and in the actions of all men, and especially of princes, which it is not prudent to challenge, one judges by the result.
cards.why: The many see the surface and the few who see through it dare not contradict the many — outcomes launder methods.
cards.uw: When a winner’s methods go unexamined.
cards.source_locator: Chapter XVIII — Concerning The Way In Which Princes Should Keep Faith

cards.book: The Prince — Niccolò Machiavelli
cards.title: Fortune favors the bold
cards.steal: For my part I consider that it is better to be adventurous than cautious, because fortune is a woman, and if you wish to keep her under it is necessary to beat and ill-use her; and it is seen that she allows herself to be mastered by the adventurous rather than by those who go to work more coldly.
cards.why: Fortune is changeful and men are steadfast in their ways; boldness is the only stance that can master chance.
cards.uw: When caution is being sold as prudence in a volatile moment.
cards.source_locator: Chapter XXV — What Fortune Can Effect In Human Affairs, And How To Withstand Her

cards.book: Meditations — Marcus Aurelius
cards.title: The morning briefing
cards.steal: Betimes in the morning say to thyself, This day I shalt have to do with an idle curious man, with an unthankful man, a railer, a crafty, false, or an envious man; an unsociable uncharitable man.
cards.why: Pre-decide your response to difficult people before the day starts — the obstacle named in advance loses its ambush.
cards.uw: When you walk into a day of difficult people.

cards.book: Meditations — Marcus Aurelius
cards.title: The inner citadel
cards.steal: At what time soever thou wilt, it is in thy power to retire into thyself, and to be at rest, and free from all businesses. A man cannot any whither retire better than to his own soul; he especially who is beforehand provided of such things within, which whensoever he doth withdraw himself to look in, may presently afford unto him perfect ease and tranquillity.
cards.why: The one retreat no circumstance can take: tranquillity as an inward order, not a place.
cards.uw: When escape feels like the only option.

cards.book: Meditations — Marcus Aurelius
cards.title: Get up — it is your work
cards.steal: In the morning when thou findest thyself unwilling to rise, consider with thyself presently, it is to go about a man's work that I am stirred up.
cards.why: Duty reframed as nature: you were made for the work, not the warm bed.
cards.uw: When the snooze button is winning the argument.

cards.book: Meditations — Marcus Aurelius
cards.title: The soul takes the dye of its thoughts
cards.steal: Such as thy thoughts and ordinary cogitations are, such will thy mind be in time. For the soul doth as it were receive its tincture from the fancies, and imaginations. Dye it therefore and thoroughly soak it with the assiduity of these cogitations.
cards.why: Attention is the mechanism of character: soak the mind deliberately, or it soaks up whatever surrounds it.
cards.uw: When choosing what to feed your attention.

cards.book: Meditations — Marcus Aurelius
cards.title: The best revenge
cards.steal: The best kind of revenge is, not to become like unto them.
cards.why: Retaliation is assimilation — the only clean victory is refusing the opponent’s shape.
cards.uw: When revenge feels righteous.

cards.book: Meditations — Marcus Aurelius
cards.title: See things unadorned
cards.steal: This is the carcass of a fish; this of a bird; and this of a hog. And again more generally; This phalernum, this excellent highly commended wine, is but the bare juice of an ordinary grape. This purple robe, but sheep's hairs, dyed with the blood of a shellfish.
cards.why: The Stoic stripping exercise: name things by what they physically are and the added glamour falls off.
cards.uw: When luxury or status is doing your thinking for you.

cards.book: Meditations — Marcus Aurelius
cards.title: Use the impediment
cards.steal: So may every reasonable creature, what crosses and impediments soever it meets with in the course of this mortal life, it may use them as fit and proper objects, to the furtherance of whatsoever it intended and absolutely proposed unto itself as its natural end and happiness.
cards.why: The obstacle as raw material: whatever blocks the action can be made the object of the action.
cards.uw: When a setback looks like the end of the plan.

cards.book: Meditations — Marcus Aurelius
cards.title: Nobody can hinder the right act
cards.steal: there is nobody that can hinder thee, but that thou mayest always both do and speak those things which are agreeable to that nature, whereof thou art a part.
cards.why: The inner-freedom claim: no one can stop you from doing and speaking what accords with your nature.
cards.uw: When external pressure is the excuse.

cards.book: Democracy in America — Alexis de Tocqueville
cards.title: Equality, the providential fact
cards.steal: The gradual development of the equality of conditions is therefore a providential fact, and it possesses all the characteristics of a divine decree: it is universal, it is durable, it constantly eludes all human interference, and all events as well as all men contribute to its progress.
cards.why: The book’s generative claim: equality of conditions is a divine-decree-level force no generation can check.
cards.uw: When democratic trends are treated as reversible policy choices.

cards.book: Democracy in America — Alexis de Tocqueville
cards.title: The fundamental fact
cards.steal: The more I advanced in the study of American society, the more I perceived that the equality of conditions is the fundamental fact from which all others seem to be derived, and the central point at which all my observations constantly terminated.
cards.why: Tocqueville’s method in one line: find the single fact from which all others derive.
cards.uw: When drowning in symptoms and you need the root.

cards.book: Democracy in America — Alexis de Tocqueville
cards.title: Association, the mother science
cards.steal: In democratic countries the science of association is the mother of science; the progress of all the rest depends upon the progress it has made.
cards.why: In democracies the art of associating is the master skill on which civilization depends.
cards.uw: When collective action fails and the proposed fix is a hero.
cards.source_locator: Volume II — Of the Use Which the Americans Make of Public Associations in Civil Life

cards.book: Democracy in America — Alexis de Tocqueville
cards.title: Individualism, defined
cards.steal: Individualism is a mature and calm feeling, which disposes each member of the community to sever himself from the mass of his fellow-creatures; and to draw apart with his family and his friends; so that, after he has thus formed a little circle of his own, he willingly leaves society at large to itself.
cards.why: The distinction that runs the book: individualism is a calm error of judgment, egotism a blind passion. Tocqueville coined the word for the new disease.
cards.uw: When withdrawal gets mislabeled as selfishness.
cards.source_locator: Volume II — Of Individualism in Democratic Countries

cards.book: Democracy in America — Alexis de Tocqueville
cards.title: Association against the majority
cards.steal: At the present time the liberty of association is become a necessary guarantee against the tyranny of the majority.
cards.why: The institutional answer to majority tyranny: not rights on paper but the organized habit of combining.
cards.uw: When a majority starts closing ranks.
cards.source_locator: Volume I — Of the Principal Causes Which Tend to Maintain the Democratic Republic in the United States

cards.book: Democracy in America — Alexis de Tocqueville
cards.title: Soft despotism
cards.steal: Above this race of men stands an immense and tutelary power, which takes upon itself alone to secure their gratifications, and to watch over their fate. That power is absolute, minute, regular, provident, and mild. It would be like the authority of a parent, if, like that authority, its object was to prepare men for manhood; but it seeks on the contrary to keep them in perpetual childhood
cards.why: The famous prophecy: a mild, absolute, minute power that keeps men in perpetual childhood and spares them the trouble of living.
cards.uw: When comfort is being traded for agency.
cards.source_locator: Volume II — What Sort of Despotism Democratic Nations Have to Fear

cards.book: Democracy in America — Alexis de Tocqueville
cards.title: The apprenticeship of liberty
cards.steal: It cannot be repeated too often that nothing is more fertile in prodigies than the art of being free; but there is nothing more arduous than the apprenticeship of liberty.
cards.why: Freedom is fertile but its apprenticeship is arduous — despotism’s temporary prosperity is the trap.
cards.uw: When liberty looks like too much trouble.

cards.book: Democracy in America — Alexis de Tocqueville
cards.title: The sad Americans
cards.steal: In America I saw the freest and most enlightened men, placed in the happiest circumstances which the world affords: it seemed to me as if a cloud habitually hung upon their brow, and I thought them serious and almost sad even in their pleasures.
cards.why: The paradox of prosperity: the freest men brooding over advantages they do not possess, feverishly pursuing welfare.
cards.uw: When success does not feel like it.
cards.source_locator: Volume II — Why the Americans Are Often So Restless in the Midst of Their Prosperity

cards.book: Democracy in America — Alexis de Tocqueville
cards.title: The press, last bulwark
cards.steal: but that servitude cannot be complete if the press is free: the press is the chiefest democratic instrument of freedom.
cards.why: Parliaments and popular sovereignty can coexist with servitude; a free press cannot.
cards.uw: When press freedom is treated as one liberty among many.
cards.source_locator: Volume II — Of the Press in the United States

cards.book: Propaganda — Edward L. Bernays
cards.title: The invisible government
cards.steal: The conscious and intelligent manipulation of the organized habits and opinions of the masses is an important element in democratic society. Those who manipulate this unseen mechanism of society constitute an invisible government which is the true ruling power of our country. We are governed, our minds are molded, our tastes formed, our ideas suggested, largely by men we have never heard of.
cards.why: The book’s opening thesis: democracy is governed by unseen manipulators of mass habit — a structural feature, not a conspiracy.
cards.uw: When “who really decides?” is the question.

cards.book: Propaganda — Edward L. Bernays
cards.title: The executive arm
cards.steal: Propaganda is the executive arm of the invisible government.
cards.why: Propaganda named as the operating machinery of the invisible government — every social project runs on it.
cards.uw: When someone thinks propaganda is only a wartime word.

cards.book: Propaganda — Edward L. Bernays
cards.title: Rubber-stamp minds
cards.steal: But instead of a mind, universal literacy has given him rubber stamps, rubber stamps inked with advertising slogans, with editorials, with published scientific data, with the trivialities of the tabloids and the platitudes of history, but quite innocent of original thought. Each man’s rubber stamps are the duplicates of millions of others, so that when those millions are exposed to the same stimuli, all receive identical imprints.
cards.why: Literacy did not produce independent minds; it produced identical imprints from identical stimuli — the precondition of mass persuasion.
cards.uw: When everyone suddenly agrees.

cards.book: Propaganda — Edward L. Bernays
cards.title: The intelligent minorities
cards.steal: clearly it is the intelligent minorities which need to make use of propaganda continuously and systematically. In the active proselytizing minorities in whom selfish interests and public interests coincide lie the progress and development of America. Only through the active energy of the intelligent few can the public at large become aware of and act upon new ideas. Small groups of persons can, and do, make the rest of us think what they please about a given subject.
cards.why: Bernays’s open claim: progress comes from small groups making the rest think what they please; minorities use propaganda continuously.
cards.uw: When a fringe idea goes mainstream overnight.

cards.book: Propaganda — Edward L. Bernays
cards.title: Reach the group leaders
cards.steal: To reach and persuade the group leaders who dictate the public’s thoughts and actions is likewise expensive. For this reason there is an increasing tendency to concentrate the functions of propaganda in the hands of the propaganda specialist.
cards.why: The targeting doctrine: persuade the leaders who dictate the public’s thoughts and the group follows — hence the propaganda specialist.
cards.uw: When planning how an idea actually spreads.

cards.book: Propaganda — Edward L. Bernays
cards.title: The PR counsel, defined
cards.steal: The public relations counsel, then, is the agent who, working with modern media of communication and the group formations of society, brings an idea to the consciousness of the public.
cards.why: The job description of the new profession: bringing ideas to public consciousness via media and group formations.
cards.uw: When “PR” needs distinguishing from advertising.

cards.book: Propaganda — Edward L. Bernays
cards.title: Induce our leaders to lead
cards.steal: The great political problem in our modern democracy is how to induce our leaders to lead. The dogma that the voice of the people is the voice of God tends to make elected persons the will-less servants of their constituents.
cards.why: The democratic paradox: the voice-of-God dogma makes elected men will-less servants, producing political sterility.
cards.uw: When leaders only follow polls.
cards.source_locator: Chapter VI — Propaganda and Political Leadership

cards.book: Propaganda — Edward L. Bernays
cards.title: Influence the leaders, sway the herd
cards.steal: If you can influence the leaders, either with or without their conscious coöperation, you automatically influence the group which they sway.
cards.why: Mass psychology works without the mass: man feels himself a herd member alone in his room, so moving the leader moves the group.
cards.uw: When a message needs scale without a crowd.
cards.source_locator: Chapter IV — The Psychology of Public Relations

cards.title: The five filters
cards.book: Manufacturing Consent — Noam Chomsky & Edward S. Herman
cards.steal: The essential ingredients of our propaganda model, or set of news “filters,” fall under the following headings: (1) the size, concentrated ownership, owner wealth, and profit orientation of the dominant mass-media firms; (2) advertising as the primary income source of the mass media; (3) the reliance of the media on information provided by government, business, and “experts” funded and approved by these primary sources and agents of power; (4) “flak” as a means of disciplining the media; and (5) “anticommunism” as a national religion and control mechanism. The raw material of news must pass through successive filters, leaving only the cleansed residue fit to print.
cards.why: The entire model in one paragraph: five structural filters decide what counts as news before any reporter writes a word.
cards.uw: When someone asks how propaganda works in a country with no censorship.

cards.title: Objectivity inside the filters
cards.book: Manufacturing Consent — Noam Chomsky & Edward S. Herman
cards.steal: The elite domination of the media and marginalization of dissidents that results from the operation of these filters occurs so naturally that media news people, frequently operating with complete integrity and goodwill, are able to convince themselves that they choose and interpret the news “objectively” and on the basis of professional news values.
cards.why: No conspiracy is required: sincere journalists can report objectively within limits they never chose.
cards.uw: When “but reporters mean well” is used to dismiss media critique.

cards.title: A Private Ministry of Information
cards.book: Manufacturing Consent — Noam Chomsky & Edward S. Herman
cards.steal: Ben Bagdikian stresses the fact that despite the large media numbers, the twenty-nine largest media systems account for over half of the output of newspapers, and most of the sales and audiences in magazines, broadcasting, books, and movies. He contends that these “constitute a new Private Ministry of Information and Culture” that can set the national agenda.
cards.why: Twenty-five thousand media entities, twenty-nine setting the agenda — ownership concentration as the first filter, with 1986 numbers.
cards.uw: When the sheer number of outlets is offered as proof of press freedom.

cards.title: A voting system weighted by income
cards.book: Manufacturing Consent — Noam Chomsky & Edward S. Herman
cards.steal: In short, the mass media are interested in attracting audiences with buying power, not audiences per se; it is affluent audiences that spark advertiser interest today, as in the nineteenth century. The idea that the drive for large audiences makes the mass media “democratic” thus suffers from the initial weakness that its political analogue is a voting system weighted by income!
cards.why: The advertising filter's core logic: the audience is the product, and only affluent buyers count.
cards.uw: When reach and ratings get mistaken for democratic representation.

cards.title: Excessive objectivity
cards.book: Manufacturing Consent — Noam Chomsky & Edward S. Herman
cards.steal: Barnouw notes that although at that time a great many large companies were spending money on commercials and other publicity regarding environmental problems, the documentary series failed for want of sponsors. The problem was one of excessive objectivity in the series, which included suggestions of corporate or systemic failure, whereas the corporate message “was one of reassurance.”
cards.why: An NBC environmental series died not for bias but for objectivity — sponsors wanted reassurance, not systemic failure.
cards.uw: When someone asks how advertisers shape content without issuing orders.

cards.title: The symbiotic relationship
cards.book: Manufacturing Consent — Noam Chomsky & Edward S. Herman
cards.steal: The mass media are drawn into a symbiotic relationship with powerful sources of information by economic necessity and reciprocity of interest. The media need a steady, reliable flow of the raw material of news. They have daily news demands and imperative news schedules that they must meet.
cards.why: The sourcing filter: beats, press conferences, and official leaks are cheaper than reporting — so power becomes the default source.
cards.uw: When official sources dominate a story and nobody asks why.

cards.title: Bureaucratic affinity
cards.book: Manufacturing Consent — Noam Chomsky & Edward S. Herman
cards.steal: Mark Fishman calls this “the principle of bureaucratic affinity: only other bureaucracies can satisfy the input needs of a news bureaucracy.”
cards.why: Why the White House, the Pentagon, and city hall are the permanent news beats: newsrooms are bureaucracies that can only feed on other bureaucracies.
cards.uw: When mapping why some voices are always quoted and others never are.

cards.title: Flak as discipline
cards.book: Manufacturing Consent — Noam Chomsky & Edward S. Herman
cards.steal: “Flak” refers to negative responses to a media statement or program. It may take the form of letters, telegrams, phone calls, petitions, lawsuits, speeches and bills before Congress, and other modes of complaint, threat, and punitive action. If certain kinds of fact, position, or program are thought likely to elicit flak, this prospect can be a deterrent.
cards.why: The fourth filter: punishment doesn't have to arrive — the anticipation of it is enough to kill a story.
cards.uw: When a story dies quietly and nobody gave an order.

cards.title: The fuzzy enemy
cards.book: Manufacturing Consent — Noam Chomsky & Edward S. Herman
cards.steal: This ideology helps mobilize the populace against an enemy, and because the concept is fuzzy it can be used against anybody advocating policies that threaten property interests or support accommodation with Communist states and radicalism.
cards.why: The fifth filter's genius: a fuzzy enemy label that can be aimed at anyone who threatens property interests.
cards.uw: When a vague ideological label gets deployed against a domestic policy.

cards.title: The commissar instruction
cards.book: Manufacturing Consent — Noam Chomsky & Edward S. Herman
cards.steal: The mass media never explain why Andrei Sakharov is worthy and José Luis Massera, in Uruguay, is unworthy—the attention and general dichotomization occur “naturally” as a result of the working of the filters, but the result is the same as if a commissar had instructed the media: “Concentrate on the victims of enemy powers and forget about the victims of friends.”
cards.why: The book's most quoted line: dichotomization happens naturally, but lands exactly where a censor's order would.
cards.uw: When coverage of foreign victims tracks official enemies and friends.

cards.title: Worthy and unworthy victims
cards.book: Manufacturing Consent — Noam Chomsky & Edward S. Herman
cards.steal: A propaganda system will consistently portray people abused in enemy states as worthy victims, whereas those treated with equal or greater severity by its own government or clients will be unworthy.
cards.why: The paired-comparison method of the whole book: worth is assigned by politics, read off the volume and tone of coverage.
cards.uw: When comparing how two similar atrocities get covered.

cards.title: Pol Pot's changing worth
cards.book: Manufacturing Consent — Noam Chomsky & Edward S. Herman
cards.steal: The victims of Pol Pot, a Communist leader, were worthy, although after he was ousted by the Vietnamese in 1978, Cambodians ceased to be worthy, as U.S. policy shifted toward support of Pol Pot in exile.
cards.why: The same dead, worthy then unworthy: victimhood tracks U.S. policy shifts, not the scale of suffering.
cards.uw: When a victim group suddenly drops out of the news.

cards.title: Demonstration elections
cards.book: Manufacturing Consent — Noam Chomsky & Edward S. Herman
cards.steal: The United States organized what have been called “demonstration elections” in its client states, defined as those whose primary function is to convince the home population that the intervention is well intentioned, that the populace of the invaded and occupied country welcomes the intrusion, and that they are being given a democratic choice.
cards.why: Elections as stagecraft for the home audience: El Salvador's vote legitimized, Nicaragua's delegitimized, by the same press.
cards.uw: When a foreign election is sold as proof of democracy.
cards.source_locator: Chapter 3 — Legitimizing versus Meaningless Third World Elections

cards.title: No conspiracy required
cards.book: Manufacturing Consent — Noam Chomsky & Edward S. Herman
cards.steal: We do not use any kind of “conspiracy” hypothesis to explain massmedia performance. In fact, our treatment is much closer to a “free market” analysis, with the results largely an outcome of the workings of market forces. Most biased choices in the media arise from the preselection of right-thinking people, internalized preconceptions, and the adaptation of personnel to the constraints of ownership, organization, market, and political power. Censorship is largely self-censorship, by reporters and commentators who adjust to the realities of source and media organizational requirements.
cards.why: The authors' preemptive defense: this is market analysis, not conspiracy — bias comes from hiring, habit, and self-censorship.
cards.uw: When the model gets dismissed as a conspiracy theory.

cards.title: Fixing the premises of discourse
cards.book: Manufacturing Consent — Noam Chomsky & Edward S. Herman
cards.steal: The special importance of propaganda in what Walter Lippmann referred to as the “manufacture of consent” has long been recognized by writers on public opinion, propaganda, and the political requirements of social order. The powerful are able to fix the premises of discourse, to decide what the general populace is allowed to see, hear, and think about, and to “manage” public opinion by regular propaganda campaigns.
cards.why: The title's thesis: power doesn't need to win arguments — it sets what arguments are allowed to happen.
cards.uw: When the debate feels lively but the boundaries feel fixed.

cards.title: Power is what the enemy thinks you have
cards.book: Rules for Radicals — Saul D. Alinsky
cards.steal: Always remember the first rule of power tactics: Power is not only what you have but what the enemy thinks you have.
cards.why: Power is perception: the size of your force is measured in the enemy's head, not in your headcount.
cards.uw: When you're outnumbered and need to look bigger than you are.

cards.title: Never go outside the experience of your people
cards.book: Rules for Radicals — Saul D. Alinsky
cards.steal: The second rule is: Never go outside the experience of your people. When an action or tactic is outside the experience of the people, the result is confusion, fear, and retreat. It also means a collapse of communication, as we have noted.
cards.why: Novelty in tactics backfires on your own side first — your people retreat before the enemy even reacts.
cards.uw: Before trying a tactic your people have never seen before.

cards.title: Go outside the experience of the enemy
cards.book: Rules for Radicals — Saul D. Alinsky
cards.steal: The third rule is: Wherever possible go outside of the experience of the enemy. Here you want to cause confusion, fear, and retreat.
cards.why: The mirror of rule two: unfamiliar tactics are a weapon only when pointed at the other side.
cards.uw: When you're planning how the enemy will react to something new.

cards.title: Make the enemy live up to its own book of rules
cards.book: Rules for Radicals — Saul D. Alinsky
cards.steal: The fourth rule is: Make the enemy live up to their own book of rules. You can kill them with this, for they can no more obey their own rules than the Christian church can live up to Christianity.
cards.why: No institution can survive full compliance with its own stated standards — so demand exactly that.
cards.uw: When an institution preaches one thing and practices another.

cards.title: Ridicule is man's most potent weapon
cards.book: Rules for Radicals — Saul D. Alinsky
cards.steal: The fourth rule carries within it the fifth rule: Ridicule is man's most potent weapon. It is almost impossible to counterattack ridicule. Also it infuriates the opposition, who then react to your advantage.
cards.why: Laughter can't be answered with a press release — and an angry opponent makes your mistakes for you.
cards.uw: When the other side's dignity is its armor.

cards.title: A good tactic is one your people enjoy
cards.book: Rules for Radicals — Saul D. Alinsky
cards.steal: The sixth rule is: A good tactic is one that your people enjoy. If your people are not having a ball doing it, there is something very wrong with the tactic.
cards.why: Fun is a tactical diagnostic — enjoyment sustains action longer than duty does.
cards.uw: When participation is flagging and you can't figure out why.

cards.title: A tactic that drags on too long becomes a drag
cards.book: Rules for Radicals — Saul D. Alinsky
cards.steal: The seventh rule: A tactic that drags on too long becomes a drag. Man can sustain militant interest in any issue for only a limited time, after which it becomes a ritualistic commitment, like going to church on Sunday mornings.
cards.why: Energy has a shelf life — a stale tactic keeps the form of action while the life drains out of it.
cards.uw: When a campaign is running on habit instead of heat.

cards.title: Keep the pressure on
cards.book: Rules for Radicals — Saul D. Alinsky
cards.steal: The eighth rule: Keep the pressure on, with different tactics and actions, and utilize all events of the period for your purpose.
cards.why: Relief is the enemy's recovery time — variety of attack keeps the opposition from ever resetting.
cards.uw: When the other side is hoping you'll get tired.

cards.title: The threat is more terrifying than the thing itself
cards.book: Rules for Radicals — Saul D. Alinsky
cards.steal: The ninth rule: The threat is usually more terrifying than the thing itself.
cards.why: Imagination does the work of force — the enemy's fear of what you might do outruns anything you could actually do.
cards.uw: When you have leverage but not the strength to spend it.

cards.title: Constant pressure produces the reaction
cards.book: Rules for Radicals — Saul D. Alinsky
cards.steal: The tenth rule: The major premise for tactics is the development of operations that will maintain a constant pressure upon the opposition. It is this unceasing pressure that results in the reactions from the opposition that are essential for the success of the campaign.
cards.why: The action is in the reaction — you don't win exchanges, you keep the enemy reacting, because reactions are what you steer.
cards.uw: When you're designing a campaign as a sequence, not a single event.

cards.title: Push a negative until it breaks into its counterside
cards.book: Rules for Radicals — Saul D. Alinsky
cards.steal: The eleventh rule is: If you push a negative hard and deep enough it will break through into its counterside; this is based on the principle that every positive has its negative.
cards.why: Overextension flips: push the enemy's attack far enough and it becomes your asset — panic makes them burglarize your office and leave their fingerprints everywhere.
cards.uw: When the opposition is overreaching and about to discredit itself.

cards.title: A successful attack needs a constructive alternative
cards.book: Rules for Radicals — Saul D. Alinsky
cards.steal: The twelfth rule: The price of a successful attack is a constructive alternative. You cannot risk being trapped by the enemy in his sudden agreement with your demand and saying “You’re right—we don’t know what to do about this issue. Now you tell us.”
cards.why: Winning the argument without an answer hands you the problem — surrender can be the enemy's best counterattack.
cards.uw: Before you demand something, have the replacement ready.

cards.title: Pick the target, freeze it, personalize it, polarize it
cards.book: Rules for Radicals — Saul D. Alinsky
cards.steal: The thirteenth rule: Pick the target, freeze it, personalize it, and polarize it.
cards.why: Institutions survive by diffusing responsibility until attack is impossible — so you pin one name to the evil and never let it squirm free.
cards.uw: When everyone's responsible and therefore no one is.

cards.title: The immaculate conception of ends
cards.book: Rules for Radicals — Saul D. Alinsky
cards.steal: The man of action views the issue of means and ends in pragmatic and strategic terms. He has no other problem; he thinks only of his actual resources and the possibilities of various choices of action. He asks of ends only whether they are achievable and worth the cost; of means, only whether they will work. To say that corrupt means corrupt the ends is to believe in the immaculate conception of ends and principles. The real arena is corrupt and bloody.
cards.why: Alinsky's ethics: judge tactics by whether they work and whether the end is worth it — purity of means is a luxury of observers, not actors.
cards.uw: When someone demands clean hands in a dirty fight.

cards.title: The Haves, the Have-Nots, and the Have-a-Little, Want Mores
cards.book: Rules for Radicals — Saul D. Alinsky
cards.steal: Mankind has been and is divided into three parts: the Haves, the Have-Nots, and the Have-a-Little, Want Mores.
cards.why: Every power fight runs on this trinity — the comfortable freeze the status quo, the desperate want to take, and the middle class wants change without risk.
cards.uw: When you're mapping who actually has a stake in changing things.

cards.title: The organizer builds power for others to use
cards.book: Rules for Radicals — Saul D. Alinsky
cards.steal: This is the basic difference between the leader and the organizer. The leader goes on to build power to fulfill his desires, to hold and wield the power for purposes both social and personal. He wants power himself. The organizer finds his goal in creation of power for others to use.
cards.why: Leadership accumulates power; organizing distributes it — the organizer's product is other people's power, not his own.
cards.uw: When you're tempted to become the leader instead of the builder.

cards.title: They were being laughed at, and this was insufferable
cards.book: Rules for Radicals — Saul D. Alinsky
cards.steal: I looked blank and replied, “Maybe I am innocent and uninformed of what has been happening here, but as far as I know the only thing Eastman Kodak has done on the race issue in America has been to introduce color film.” The reaction was shock, anger, and resentment from Kodak. They were not being attacked or insulted—they were being laughed at, and this was insufferable.
cards.why: Ridicule in the field: Kodak could survive attack but not laughter — the fifth rule demonstrated on the most powerful company in Rochester.
cards.uw: When you need proof that ridicule works on the powerful.

cards.title: The three rebalancings
cards.book: Machine, Platform, Crowd — Andrew McAfee & Erik Brynjolfsson
cards.steal: We will try to convince you that because of recent technological changes, companies need to rethink the balance between minds and machines, between products and platforms, and between the core and the crowd. The second element in each pair has become much more capable and more powerful just within the past few years, so it needs to be considered with fresh eyes.
cards.why: The book's entire thesis in one paragraph: nothing is obsolete, but the balance point in all three pairs has moved — and most companies are still calibrated to the old one.
cards.uw: When you're deciding where the next dollar of investment goes: mind or machine, product or platform, core or crowd.

cards.title: 136 studies: the formulas beat the experts
cards.book: Machine, Platform, Crowd — Andrew McAfee & Erik Brynjolfsson
cards.steal: They found 136 such studies, covering everything from prediction of IQ to diagnosis of heart disease. In 48% of them, there was no significant difference between the two; the experts, in other words, were on average no better than the formulas. A much bigger blow to the notion of human superiority in judgment came from the finding that in 46% of the studies considered, the human experts actually performed significantly worse than the numbers and formulas alone.
cards.why: Fifty years of head-to-head research, quantified: experts tie the formula half the time and lose to it nearly half the time — the empirical foundation for handing decisions to algorithms.
cards.uw: When an expert's gut says one thing and the model says another.
cards.source_locator: Chapter 2: The Hardest Thing to Accept About Ourselves

cards.title: Meehl: no controversy points so uniformly one way
cards.book: Machine, Platform, Crowd — Andrew McAfee & Erik Brynjolfsson
cards.steal: There is no controversy in social science that shows such a large body of qualitatively diverse studies coming out so uniformly in the same direction as this one [the relative validity of statistical versus clinical prediction]. When you are pushing over 100 investigations, predicting everything from the outcome of football games to the diagnosis of liver disease and when you can hardly come up with a half dozen studies showing even a weak tendency in favor of the clinician, it is time to draw a practical conclusion.
cards.why: Meehl's summary is the kill shot for expert judgment: across a hundred-plus investigations, the evidence points one direction — use the formula.
cards.uw: When someone defends expert intuition against the data.
cards.source_locator: Chapter 2: The Hardest Thing to Accept About Ourselves

cards.title: Tetlock: humanity barely bests a chimp
cards.book: Machine, Platform, Crowd — Andrew McAfee & Erik Brynjolfsson
cards.steal: In a test involving more than 82,000 forecasts, Tetlock found that “humanity barely bests [a] chimp” throwing darts at the possible outcomes.
cards.why: 82,000 expert forecasts, and the species barely beats random darts — the prediction half of the book's case against the expert core.
cards.uw: When a forecast is presented as expertise rather than a coin flip with footnotes.
cards.source_locator: Chapter 2: The Hardest Thing to Accept About Ourselves

cards.title: HiPPO: the highest-paid person's opinion
cards.book: Machine, Platform, Crowd — Andrew McAfee & Erik Brynjolfsson
cards.steal: In 2006, Avinash Kaushik and Ronny Kohavi, two data analysis professionals who were then working at Intuit and Microsoft, respectively, came up with the acronym HiPPO to summarize the dominant decision-making style at most companies. It stands for “highest-paid person’s opinion.”
cards.why: The name for the old decision regime: whoever is paid most decides most — the exact habit the data-driven rebalancing is meant to kill.
cards.uw: When a meeting is about to be decided by rank instead of evidence.
cards.source_locator: Chapter 2: The Hardest Thing to Accept About Ourselves

cards.title: Machine learning, defined
cards.book: Machine, Platform, Crowd — Andrew McAfee & Erik Brynjolfsson
cards.steal: Machine learning—the art and science of building software systems that can detect patterns and formulate winning strategies after being shown many examples—is finally fulfilling its early promise and accomplishing useful work.
cards.why: The hinge of the whole machine section: ML is pattern detection from examples, not programmed rules — which is why it suddenly started working.
cards.uw: When you need the one-sentence version of what machine learning actually is.

cards.title: AI still lacks common sense
cards.book: Machine, Platform, Crowd — Andrew McAfee & Erik Brynjolfsson
cards.steal: Machine learning systems (and all other forms of AI) still lack common sense.
cards.why: The permanent caveat on the machine section: pattern-matching at scale, yes — understanding the world, no.
cards.uw: When AI hype needs its one-sentence brake pedal.

cards.title: DANCE: the drivers of the robot explosion
cards.book: Machine, Platform, Crowd — Andrew McAfee & Erik Brynjolfsson
cards.steal: Drivers of the robotic Cambrian Explosion include data, algorithms, networks, the cloud, and exponential improvements in hardware: DANCE. Robots and their kin will be increasingly used wherever work is dull, dirty, dangerous, and dear.
cards.why: Five drivers, one acronym, one deployment rule: robots go where work is dull, dirty, dangerous, or dear — a checklist for where automation lands next.
cards.uw: When you're scanning your own industry for what gets automated first.

cards.title: Free, perfect, and instant
cards.book: Machine, Platform, Crowd — Andrew McAfee & Erik Brynjolfsson
cards.steal: The marginal cost of an additional digital copy is (almost) zero, each digital copy is a perfect replica of the original, and each digital copy can be transmitted across the planet virtually instantly.
cards.why: The three economic properties that let bits eat every industry they touch — the physics underneath the whole platform section.
cards.uw: When you're asking whether your industry is next to be digitized.
cards.source_locator: Chapter 6: The Toll of a New Machine

cards.title: A platform, defined
cards.book: Machine, Platform, Crowd — Andrew McAfee & Erik Brynjolfsson
cards.steal: A platform can be described as a digital environment characterized by near-zero marginal cost of access, reproduction, and distribution.
cards.why: The book's working definition: a platform is not an app or a website, it's an economic environment — near-zero cost to join, copy, and spread.
cards.uw: When you need to tell a platform from a product.
cards.source_locator: Chapter 6: The Toll of a New Machine

cards.title: Demand-side economies of scale
cards.book: Machine, Platform, Crowd — Andrew McAfee & Erik Brynjolfsson
cards.steal: Networked goods become more valuable as more people use them. The result is “demand-side economies of scale,” giving an advantage to bigger networks.
cards.why: The flip of industrial economics: advantage goes to the biggest network, not the biggest factory — which is why platforms tip to winner-take-most.
cards.uw: When you're sizing up why the biggest platform keeps winning.
cards.source_locator: Chapter 6: The Toll of a New Machine

cards.title: Complements: the platform's demand engine
cards.book: Machine, Platform, Crowd — Andrew McAfee & Erik Brynjolfsson
cards.steal: Two products are complements if a drop in the price of one pushes out the demand curve for the other.
cards.why: The one-line economics behind the whole platform playbook: open the platform, let outsiders build complements, watch demand for your product rise.
cards.uw: When you're deciding whether to open up or lock down.
cards.source_locator: Chapter 7: Paying Complements, and Other Smart Strategies

cards.title: The crowd is the opposite of the core
cards.book: Machine, Platform, Crowd — Andrew McAfee & Erik Brynjolfsson
cards.steal: The crowd is, in many ways, the opposite of the core: it’s huge, diverse, largely uncontrollable, and often messy.
cards.why: The third rebalance stated as a contrast: the core is built, the crowd is found — huge, diverse, uncontrollable, and increasingly more powerful than what's inside.
cards.uw: When you're weighing an internal team against the world outside it.

cards.title: The crowd beats the credentialed core, repeatedly
cards.book: Machine, Platform, Crowd — Andrew McAfee & Erik Brynjolfsson
cards.steal: Over and over again, the recognized experts of the core see their performance beaten by uncredentialed and conventionally inexperienced members of the crowd.
cards.why: The empirical claim of the crowd section: it's not a theory about openness, it's a track record of outsiders beating insiders.
cards.uw: When the experts say only experts can solve it.
cards.source_locator: Chapter 11: Why the Expert You Know Is Not the Expert You Need

cards.title: Why companies survive: incomplete contracting
cards.book: Machine, Platform, Crowd — Andrew McAfee & Erik Brynjolfsson
cards.steal: Companies and other nonmarket organizations are needed to deal with the problem of incomplete contracting—the fact that contracts cannot realistically specify all possible contingencies in the messy real world.
cards.why: The authors' answer to their own provocative chapter title: the crowd can't replace companies because contracts can't cover reality — someone has to hold the residual right to decide.
cards.uw: When decentralization hype says companies are finished.

cards.title: Ask what we want to do with technology
cards.book: Machine, Platform, Crowd — Andrew McAfee & Erik Brynjolfsson
cards.steal: So we should ask not “What will technology do to us?” but rather “What do we want to do with technology?”
cards.why: The book's closing reversal: technology is a tool, not a fate — the question was never what it does to us, but what we choose to do with it.
cards.uw: When the conversation turns fatalist about AI, platforms, or crowds.
cards.source_locator: Conclusion: Economies and Societies Beyond Computation

cards.title: Things get weird in the second half of the chessboard
cards.book: The Second Machine Age — Erik Brynjolfsson & Andrew McAfee
cards.steal: In other words, things get weird in the second half of the chessboard. And like the emperor, most of us have trouble keeping up.
cards.why: The book's master metaphor: exponential growth stays inside human intuition for the first 32 doublings, then leaves it behind entirely — which is where digital technology now lives.
cards.uw: When someone projects a technology trend in a straight line.
cards.source_locator: Chapter 3: Moore's Law and the Second Half of the Chessboard

cards.title: American business entered the second half in 2006
cards.book: The Second Machine Age — Erik Brynjolfsson & Andrew McAfee
cards.steal: U.S. businesses entered the second half of the chessboard when it comes to the use of digital gear. That was in 2006.
cards.why: Pins the metaphor to a date: counting doublings of corporate IT investment since 1958, the disorientation regime began nearly a decade before the book was written — it isn't coming, it's here.
cards.uw: When dating when the AI economy actually began.
cards.source_locator: Chapter 3: Moore's Law and the Second Half of the Chessboard

cards.title: Bounty: the best economic news in the world today
cards.book: The Second Machine Age — Erik Brynjolfsson & Andrew McAfee
cards.steal: Bounty is the increase in volume, variety, and quality and the decrease in cost of the many offerings brought on by modern technological progress. It’s the best economic news in the world today.
cards.why: The optimistic half of the book's frame, defined with precision: more stuff, better stuff, cheaper stuff — the part of the story the doomers leave out.
cards.uw: When the AI debate goes all-doom.

cards.title: Spread: ever-bigger differences in economic success
cards.book: The Second Machine Age — Erik Brynjolfsson & Andrew McAfee
cards.steal: Spread, however, is not so great; it’s ever-bigger differences among people in economic success—in wealth, income, mobility, and other important measures.
cards.why: The pessimistic half, defined with matching precision: the same technology that multiplies the bounty distributes it unevenly — and the spread is accelerating too.
cards.uw: When someone cites growth statistics that hide distribution.

cards.title: The driver is exponential, digital, and combinatorial
cards.book: The Second Machine Age — Erik Brynjolfsson & Andrew McAfee
cards.steal: Instead, the main driver is exponential, digital, and combinatorial change in the technology that undergirds our economic system.
cards.why: The authors' causal claim, ruling out the usual suspects: tax policy, trade, and Wall Street aren't the primary drivers of inequality — the technology itself is.
cards.uw: When hunting the root cause of wage stagnation.

cards.title: The Great Decoupling
cards.book: The Second Machine Age — Erik Brynjolfsson & Andrew McAfee
cards.steal: While these two key economic statistics tracked each other for most of the postwar period, they became decoupled in the late 1990s. Productivity continued its upward path as employment sagged.
cards.why: The chart that broke the postwar deal: productivity at record highs while employment and median income flatline — growth no longer lifts all boats automatically.
cards.uw: When someone says economic growth lifts all boats.
cards.source_locator: Chapter 11: Implications of the Bounty and the Spread

cards.title: We know more than we can tell
cards.book: The Second Machine Age — Erik Brynjolfsson & Andrew McAfee
cards.steal: “We know more than we can tell.”
cards.why: Polanyi's line was the great defense of human work — tacit knowledge that can't be boiled down to rules can't be computerized. The book's twist: machines learned pattern recognition anyway, and the defense is collapsing task by task.
cards.uw: When someone claims their job is safe because it needs 'human judgment.'
cards.source_locator: Chapter 2: The Skills of the New Machines

cards.title: Weak human plus machine plus better process
cards.book: The Second Machine Age — Erik Brynjolfsson & Andrew McAfee
cards.steal: Weak human + machine + better process was superior to a strong computer alone and, more remarkably, superior to a strong human + machine + inferior process.
cards.why: Freestyle chess proved the formula: process beats both raw talent and raw compute. The amateurs with three laptops beat grandmasters with supercomputers — how you combine with the machine matters more than either side alone.
cards.uw: When designing how your team actually uses AI tools.
cards.source_locator: Chapter 12: Learning to Race with Machines

cards.title: Race with machines, not against them
cards.book: The Second Machine Age — Erik Brynjolfsson & Andrew McAfee
cards.steal: people still have a great deal to offer the game of chess at its highest levels once they’re allowed to race with machines, instead of purely against them.
cards.why: The book's answer to automation anxiety: the winning move is partnership, not competition. Humans contribute strategic guidance; machines contribute tactical acuity — and the combination beats both.
cards.uw: When the automation debate turns zero-sum.
cards.source_locator: Chapter 12: Learning to Race with Machines

cards.title: Close enough to zero to create strange economics
cards.book: The Second Machine Age — Erik Brynjolfsson & Andrew McAfee
cards.steal: While the marginal costs of digital goods do not quite approach zero, they are close enough to create some pretty strange economics.
cards.why: Near-zero marginal cost is the engine under winner-take-all: one producer with a website can serve billions, so capacity constraints — the thing that used to spread markets around — become irrelevant.
cards.uw: When explaining why digital markets concentrate into monopolies.
cards.source_locator: Chapter 10: The Biggest Winners: Stars and Superstars

cards.title: Free news that shrinks GDP
cards.book: The Second Machine Age — Erik Brynjolfsson & Andrew McAfee
cards.steal: replacing a paid newspaper with an equivalent free news service would decrease GDP even though it increased consumer surplus.
cards.why: The measurement crisis in one sentence: GDP counts paid transactions, not wellbeing, so the digital bounty — free, better, everywhere — is invisible to the scoreboard we run the economy on.
cards.uw: When GDP says the economy is fine but life feels better than the numbers.

cards.title: Possibilities do not merely add up; they multiply
cards.book: The Second Machine Age — Erik Brynjolfsson & Andrew McAfee
cards.steal: Possibilities do not merely add up; they multiply.
cards.why: Romer's recombinant engine, adopted as the book's theory of innovation: digital networks let ideas combine and recombine without limit, so the innovation pool compounds instead of depleting.
cards.uw: When someone argues we've run out of big ideas.

cards.title: Give people money
cards.book: The Second Machine Age — Erik Brynjolfsson & Andrew McAfee
cards.steal: Many of them have proposed the same simple solution: give people money.
cards.why: The authors' long-term answer to spread: basic income — an equal yearly payment, no means testing — with a lineage from Thomas Paine to MLK, as the way to share the bounty when labor alone can't.
cards.uw: When the conversation turns to what happens if the jobs don't come back.

cards.title: The future depends on the choices we make
cards.book: The Second Machine Age — Erik Brynjolfsson & Andrew McAfee
cards.steal: Technology creates possibilities and potential, but ultimately, the future we get will depend on the choices we make.
cards.why: The closing rejection of technological determinism: the second machine age hands us vastly more power to change the world, and with it the responsibility to choose what kind of world — bounty shared or disaster.
cards.uw: When the AI future is framed as inevitable.

cards.book: TradeBook: How to Build a Complete Trading System (Stock Market Trading and Investing) — Crede Sheehy-Kelly & Andrew Aziz
cards.title: A strategy is a concept; a TradeBook is a manual
cards.steal: There is a fundamental difference between a strategy and a TradeBook. A strategy outlines the overall concept—what to look for in a particular type of trade and how that trade generally works. A TradeBook, however, is much more practical, more like a manual.
cards.why: The book's spine sentence: a strategy only says what to look for, a TradeBook scripts selection, identification, planning, entries, exits, stops, position sizing, management, and psychology.
cards.uw: When someone pitches a 'strategy' with no rules for entries, exits, or review.

cards.book: TradeBook: How to Build a Complete Trading System (Stock Market Trading and Investing) — Crede Sheehy-Kelly & Andrew Aziz
cards.title: The edge is the combination, not one piece
cards.steal: The edge in trading doesn’t come from any one of these pieces on their own. It comes from combining them into a system that works for you. That’s what a TradeBook helps you build—a personalized, complete, and practical trading guide based on your tools, your mindset, and your strategy.
cards.why: Technology, strategy, and psychology each fail alone; the TradeBook is the overlap where all three meet, and that overlap is the only durable edge.
cards.uw: When a trader keeps buying better tools instead of building a system.

cards.book: TradeBook: How to Build a Complete Trading System (Stock Market Trading and Investing) — Crede Sheehy-Kelly & Andrew Aziz
cards.title: Gamification traded against the retail trader
cards.steal: A November 2024 study shed light on this trend, analyzing 142 gamification features in the mobile trading apps of 17 major U.S. brokers. The research found that while these features successfully increased retail trading activity and income for brokers and market makers, they often led to lower returns and higher volatility for the retail traders themselves.
cards.why: The technology chapter's warning: the tools were built to increase broker income, and they work — by making you trade more and win less.
cards.uw: When a flashy app makes trading feel like a game and you trade more than planned.

cards.book: TradeBook: How to Build a Complete Trading System (Stock Market Trading and Investing) — Crede Sheehy-Kelly & Andrew Aziz
cards.title: Consistent hours, consistent results
cards.steal: The consistency of your trading hours has a direct impact on the consistency of your results.
cards.why: A one-line case for routine as infrastructure: concentrated volatility at defined hours lets a retail trader be sharp; 24/7 markets invite 24/7 bleed.
cards.uw: When your trading day has no edges and neither do your results.

cards.book: TradeBook: How to Build a Complete Trading System (Stock Market Trading and Investing) — Crede Sheehy-Kelly & Andrew Aziz
cards.title: Sitting out is a skill
cards.steal: Recognizing when not to trade is as valuable as knowing when to take a position.
cards.why: Most price action is choppy with no clear winner; the discipline to wait for a readable signal is priced like an entry skill.
cards.uw: When you feel the pull to trade an ambiguous tape.
cards.source_locator: Chapter 3: Understanding Price Action and Developing Well-Defined Strategies

cards.book: TradeBook: How to Build a Complete Trading System (Stock Market Trading and Investing) — Crede Sheehy-Kelly & Andrew Aziz
cards.title: Your edge is a TradeBook, codified and identifiable
cards.steal: Bear Bull Traders calls your edge in the markets your “TradeBooks”, and we define your edge as a specific market opportunity codified in a specific TradeBook, which is repeatedly identifiable, and provides you with a positive expected value in profit, over time, when executed with discipline.
cards.why: The formal definition: an edge is not a feeling about a setup, it is an opportunity written down, repeatedly recognizable, and positive-expectancy — the casino model of trading.
cards.uw: When asked to name your edge and you can only describe vibes.
cards.source_locator: Chapter 4: Building and Executing a TradeBook

cards.book: TradeBook: How to Build a Complete Trading System (Stock Market Trading and Investing) — Crede Sheehy-Kelly & Andrew Aziz
cards.title: The TradeBook answers: should I take this trade?
cards.steal: If you cannot put the trade opportunity into any of your TradeBooks, it means you should not take that trade. And this is the most important purpose of your TradeBooks. They help you answer the question: Should I take the trade or not?
cards.why: The TradeBook's gatekeeping function: it converts 'this looks good' into a binary fit-or-skip decision, which is where most retail losses begin.
cards.uw: When a tempting setup does not quite fit your plan but you want it anyway.
cards.source_locator: Chapter 4: Building and Executing a TradeBook

cards.book: TradeBook: How to Build a Complete Trading System (Stock Market Trading and Investing) — Crede Sheehy-Kelly & Andrew Aziz
cards.title: Success is not being right most of the time
cards.steal: This highlights a vital aspect of trading: success is not about being right most of the time. Instead, it is about ensuring that your winning trades are large enough to outweigh your losses.
cards.why: Seven years of ORB research: stopped out 75% of the time, profitable on 25%, and still beating the market — expectancy, not win rate, is the scoreboard.
cards.uw: When a low win rate tempts you to abandon a working system.
cards.source_locator: Chapter 4: Building and Executing a TradeBook

cards.book: TradeBook: How to Build a Complete Trading System (Stock Market Trading and Investing) — Crede Sheehy-Kelly & Andrew Aziz
cards.title: Drawdowns are asymmetric: 50% down needs 100% to recover
